entry.evidence: We present an approach for extracting quantifiable information from archival aerial photographs to extend the temporal record of change

steps.action: Frame the open question of whether the many small, little-studied Greenland outlets change homogeneously with the ice sheet, against the prevailing tendency to assume so.
steps.quote: it had been tempting to infer that change in this multitude of relatively poorly studied smaller outlets was homogeneous

steps.action: Propose Structure-from-Motion processing of 1930s BAARE oblique survey photographs to build georeferenced orthophotos that extend the glacier record before satellites.
steps.quote: we utilize Structure from Motion (SfM) approaches to build georeferenced orthophotos of the terrain within the BAARE imagery

steps.action: Add the aim of identifying the drivers of glacier change from air temperature, SST and mass balance records.
steps.quote: we also explore changes in air temperature, sea surface temperature, and mass balance in an effort to identify the drivers of glacier change here

steps.action: Assemble three archival photo sets covering 24 glaciers: 73 BAARE oblique plates (1930-31), CORONA KH-4 stereo images (1966) and 58 Danish vertical aerial images (1981).
steps.quote: we used three sets of photographic data

steps.action: Choose the ArcticDEM 2 m mosaic over day-stamped strips as ground truth, place GCPs on stable bare ground, and build orthophotomaps per sub-region in Agisoft Metashape using all available images.
steps.quote: Thus we decided to use the 2 m mosaic.

steps.action: Check georeferencing accuracy of the orthophotomaps against ArcticDEM GCPs (about 1 pixel, under 20 m) and bound isostatic-uplift error with GIA models (at most 18 cm).
steps.quote: The GCP placement accuracy calculated during the processing of the mosaics was around 1 pixel

steps.action: Add Landsat 5, 7 and 8 composites for 1985, 1995, 2005, 2015 and 2019, chosen in July-August with minimal cloud.
steps.quote: we use satellite records to explore glacier change from 1985 to the present day

steps.action: Delineate margins manually, measure centre-line length change across seven time steps, convert to m per year, and propagate orthomosaic errors into RMSE (26-39 m).
steps.quote: we use contemporary velocity data to define a centre-line and measure a single length change

steps.action: Compile Tasilaaq air temperature and PDD, HadISST sea surface temperature, and a small fjord bathymetry set, relative to a 1951-1980 baseline after Box et al. (2009).
steps.quote: were acquired from a meteorological station maintained by the Danish Meteorological Institute at Tasilaaq

steps.action: Use modelled SE Greenland surface mass balance from other groups' reconstructions (Wake et al. 2009; Box and Colgan 2013).
steps.quote: Here we utilize modelled surface mass balance data

steps.action: Establish that all glaciers retreated overall from 1930 to 2019, with mid-century advance phases and accelerated recent retreat; marine-terminating glaciers vary more than land-terminating and local glaciers (Figures 3-6, Table 2).
steps.quote: all glaciers in our study area experienced overall retreat

steps.action: Describe the climate records as four cool-warm-cool-warm periods, with SST damped and lagging air temperature and SMB not tracking either simply (Figure 7).
steps.quote: Both air temperature and SST show the same broad trends

steps.action: Compare the timing of frontal advance and retreat with the climate periods qualitatively, allowing a lagged response.
steps.quote: We also observe these external forcings playing out in the changing extent of the outlets

steps.action: Retain air and ocean temperature as the regional driver of the overall glacier trend.
steps.quote: This suggests that the underlying drivers of these changes are air and ocean temperatures.

steps.action: Set their SST observations against Wood et al. (2021) on warm Atlantic water intrusion, noting they lack subsurface temperature data.
steps.quote: Our observations in relation to SST are in close keeping with recent work by

steps.action: Hypothesize that warming ocean waters contribute importantly to the observed mass loss.
steps.quote: We hypothesize that warming ocean waters may well play an important role in the mass loss we observe.

steps.action: Establish local heterogeneity: neighbouring glaciers of the same type under the same forcing behave very differently.
steps.quote: glaciers that are close neighbours and are of the same type can also show very different behaviour

steps.action: List non-climatic rival controls from the literature: ice velocity, ocean circulation, bed topography and bathymetry, sea ice, and ice thickness.
steps.quote: Therefore differing responses implies there are significant additional processes in operation.

steps.action: Trace detailed frontal histories of Glaciers 7-10, 14 and 15 with velocity overlays, showing stable outlets next to outlets with stepwise retreat.
steps.quote: Glacier 10 showed relatively modest retreat from 1930 to 2015, but then large-scale and rapid retreat in the 4 years to 2019

steps.action: Adapt Wood et al.'s shallow-ridge explanation: stable glaciers sit on pinning ridges or in shallow water, and retreat steps mark moves off ridges into deeper water.
steps.quote: we propose that these understudied glaciers also sit on ridges and/or in shallow water

steps.action: Compare bathymetry in front of Glacier 14: the stable western part is in deeper water, against expectation, but closer inspection shows a subtle shallowing that may be a pinning ridge.
steps.quote: directly in front of the western part of this glacier, there is a subtle shallowing of the bed

steps.action: Invoke ice velocity as an auxiliary: high velocity offsets calving in the west, and low velocity fails to offset it in the shallower east.
steps.quote: it is also possible that the apparent relative stability of the western outlet arises because comparatively high calving rates are offset by higher ice velocities

steps.action: Support the topographic-control reading with Porter et al. (2018b) and Catania et al. (2018), and argue that regional divisions mask glacier-scale complexity.
steps.quote: Similar to our findings, they also showed that taking account of the presence of shallow sills was important

steps.action: Conclude that responses are highly variable, with climate as the broad driver and shallow pinning ridges as a proposed control on marine-terminating variability.
steps.quote: one of our primary conclusions is that there is enormous variability in how glaciers respond to the climatic and non-climatic drivers

tree.answer: 90-year frontal retreat of 24 small East Greenland glaciers, heterogeneous among neighbours
Front positions observed directly in orthophotos; drivers (climate, bathymetry) not observed directly
Extend the record before satellites and identify the drivers of change
Climatic forcing (air temperature, SST, SMB) versus non-climatic controls (bathymetry and ridges, velocity, sea ice, thickness)
Partly: neighbours under the same forcing should respond alike if climate alone acts; no quantitative predictions
Conditions found in archival snapshots, not set

tree.answer: Yes: 24 glaciers under shared forcing over seven time steps
Only georeferencing accuracy and uplift error checked; the interpretation is not varied
Climate kept as broad driver; ridge control proposed as best explanation, largely untested

end.claim: Small East Greenland outlets retreated over 1930-2019 under broad climatic (air and ocean temperature) forcing, but with strong glacier-to-glacier heterogeneity, plausibly controlled by shallow pinning ridges in submarine topography.

decisive_move.sentence: Without SfM orthorectification of the 1930s BAARE oblique plates (and the 1966 CORONA images) there would be no pre-satellite frontal record and no 90-year heterogeneity claim.

gates.evidence: The key imagery was collected in 1930-1981 for surveying and intelligence, and datasets were chosen by availability, not by hypothesis. The climate-driver claim faces only a qualitative timing comparison (§3.5 ¶4). The ridge hypothesis is tested only at Glacier 14, where the first look mismatched and an auxiliary (velocity) was added (§4.2 ¶5); most glaciers have no bathymetry (§4.2 ¶4). Nothing is stated as fixed in advance apart from the cited 1951-1980 baseline (§2.5.1 ¶1).

imports.item: Declassified CORONA KH-4 satellite stereo imagery
1930-31 British Arctic Air Route Expedition survey photographs

novelty_claims.quote: this suite of data provides unprecedented insights into the changes that have taken place over > 90 years
This is unique to our study because this area is relatively little studied
The novelty of our work is not only the exploration of previously unstudied, smaller outlets in East Greenland
Our study covers ∼ 90 years and is the first such dedicated study in this region and over this duration.

limits: No review file or discussion was supplied, so no review sequence was coded, although the paper went through TCD open discussion and thanks the editor and three referees. Sub-claims at other statuses: the archival SfM pipeline is capability_characterized (§5 ¶1, accuracy in Table 1 and §2.2 ¶2); the frontal-change rates are estimate_with_resolution (Table 2 errors, §2.4 ¶1); the warming-ocean role is a hypothesis without subsurface data (§4.1 ¶2); the pinning-ridge control is acknowledged as speculative (§4.2 ¶2) and is checked against bathymetry at one glacier only (§4.2 ¶5). The climate-glacier link rests on visual period matching, with no statistical test (inference). The southern region has no data before 1985 (§3.1 ¶3). Each glacier is measured at a single centre-line point. The Figure 7 caption attributes the SMB series to Mittivakkat Gletscher, while the text describes modelled SE Greenland SMB, an internal inconsistency. No code is released (Code availability). The walk also has capability_first features (entry by capability), but rivals are posed before the phenomenon is established, so trace_series was chosen.

disagreements.target: The inference, from ice-sheet-wide analyses (Moon et al., 2020), that smaller outlets change homogeneously
disagreements.support: Glacier-by-glacier frontal records over 90 years show divergent behaviour even among adjacent glaciers of the same type.
disagreements.quote: it had been tempting to infer that change in this multitude of relatively poorly studied smaller outlets was homogeneous

disagreements.target: Regional divisions of the GrIS (Mouginot et al., 2019; King et al., 2020) as the frame for understanding response
disagreements.support: Neighbouring glaciers within one region show markedly different retreat patterns (Figures 8 and 9).
disagreements.quote: Such diverse observations highlight how even dividing the ice sheet up into regions masks the complexity that is inherent in individual glacier behaviour.

disagreements.target: Hanna et al. (2021): Greenland air temperature trends flat since 2001
disagreements.support: The Tasilaaq record is flat after 2001 in isolation but rises over the contemporary period as a whole, especially minimum temperatures.
disagreements.quote: However, considering the contemporary period as a whole, we believe that temperature trends do show an overall increasing trend.
